mainTopic: When one must give up his life in public (פרהסיא), why אסתר did not, and whether a בן נח is commanded in קידוש השם
overview: This amud finishes the rule that during a decree against Judaism, one must give up his life rather than change even a sandal strap. The גמרא then asks how many people make an act public (פרהסיא). רבי יוחנן says ten, and a ברייתא uses a גזירה שוה on the word 'תוך' to show that all ten must be Jews. The גמרא challenges this from אסתר, whose relationship with the king was public, yet she did not give up her life. אביי answers that she was completely passive, like the ground. רבא answers that when a non-Jew forces a sin for his own benefit, it is different. רבא proves this from the coal shovels Jews handed to the Persians, and the גמרא shows that this matches רבא's own ruling about cutting grass on שבת. Finally, the חכמים ask whether a בן נח must give up his life for קידוש השם. אביי's proof from the seven מצוות is rejected, and the school of רב brings the story of נעמן and אלישע, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Even a sandal strap during a decree
steps.stepSummary: The end of a statement from the previous daf: during a government decree against Jewish practice, one must give up his life rather than change even the strap of his sandal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even to change the strap of a sandal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a teaching that started on the previous daf. In a time of שמד, a government decree against Judaism, one must accept death rather than change even a small Jewish custom like a sandal strap.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally only the three cardinal sins require יהרג ואל יעבור. During a decree aimed at making Jews abandon their religion, even the smallest custom becomes a test of loyalty to the תורה. So even changing the style of a sandal strap to match the non-Jews is forbidden at the cost of one's life.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a rule for ordinary private situations. It applies when the act would be done in public, before ten Jews, or when a government makes a decree whose goal is to force Jews to give up their religion.

phrases.english: Even to change the strap of a sandal.
phrases.notes: This finishes a line from the previous daf about a time of government decrees. Jews had their own style of sandal strap, and here one may not switch to the non-Jewish style.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a statement begun on the previous daf about יהרג ואל יעבור in a time of decree.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a time of government decree, one must give up his life rather than change even a minor Jewish custom such as a sandal strap.

steps.title: How many people make it public?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how many people must be present for an act to count as פרהסיא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how many people make it 'public'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the word פרהסיא from the earlier discussion. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier on the daf, the rule was that in public one must give up his life even for a minor מצוה. To apply that rule, we need to know exactly what counts as 'public'.

phrases.english: And how many make it public?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the case of a decree to defining what counts as a public setting.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The minimum number of people needed for an act to be considered public.

steps.title: Public means at least ten people
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב, quoting רבי יוחנן, answers that an act is not public with fewer than ten people.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב said in the name of רבי יוחנן: 'Public' is not fewer than ten people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: an act counts as public only if at least ten people are present.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sets a clear number. With fewer than ten people, the act is treated as private, and the stricter public rule does not apply.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yaakov said that Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין פַּרְהֶסְיָא פְּחוּתָה מֵעֲשָׂרָה בְּנֵי אָדָם.
phrases.english: Public is not fewer than ten people.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: At least ten people are needed for an act to be public.

steps.title: Obviously the ten must be Jews
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says it is obvious the ten must be Jews, because the פסוק says 'among the children of Israel'.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious that we need Jews, as it is written: 'And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a point it treats as obvious: the ten people must be Jews.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source for קידוש השם is the פסוק 'ונקדשתי בתוך בני ישראל'. Since it says 'בני ישראל', the people present must be Jewish. This sets up the next question about a mixed group.

phrases.english: It is obvious that we need Jews,
as it is written: "And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a detail to the definition of ten: they must be Jews.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ten people who make an act public must be Jews, based on 'בתוך בני ישראל'.

steps.title: Nine Jews and one non-Jew
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks what the law is if nine Jews and one non-Jew are present.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked: Nine Jews and one non-Jew, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה asks about a mixed group. Do we need all ten to be Jews, or is it enough that most of them are?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 said Jews are needed, but did not say whether every single one must be Jewish. This in-between case tests how strict the requirement is.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya asked:
Nine Jews and one non-Jew, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the limits of the 'Jews' requirement from step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a group of nine Jews and one non-Jew counts as public.

steps.title: All ten must be Jews, learned from 'among'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא of רב ינאי uses a גזירה שוה on the word 'תוך' to prove that all ten must be Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear what רב ינאי, brother of רבי חייא בר אבא, taught: We learn 'among' from 'among'. Here it says 'And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel', and there it says 'Separate yourselves from among this congregation.' Just as there it was ten, all Jews, so too here it is ten, all Jews.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רבי ירמיה from a ברייתא: all ten must be Jews, so nine Jews and one non-Jew do not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'תוך' appears both in the פסוק of קידוש השם and in the story of קרח's group, which is called an 'עדה'. That 'עדה' is linked to the ten spies, a group of ten that were all Jews. So the 'among' of קידוש השם also means ten Jews, every one of them.

keyTerms.meaning: Just as there, so too here

steps.whatToRemember: פרהסיא means at least ten people, and all ten must be Jews.

phrases.english: Come and hear, for Rav Yannai taught,
the brother of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba:
We learn "among" from "among":
It is written here: "And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel,"
and it is written there: "Separate yourselves from among this congregation."
phrases.notes: במדבר 16:21, said about קרח and his group.

phrases.english: Just as there it is ten, and all of them Jews,
phrases.notes: Where does ten come from? The ten spies are also called an 'evil עדה' (במדבר 14:27).

phrases.english: so too here it is ten, and all of them Jews.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּתָנֵי רַב יַנַּאי אֲחוּהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves רבי ירמיה's question from step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: All ten must be Jews, so nine Jews and one non-Jew is not public.
steps.raayaObject: רבי ירמיה's question about a mixed group
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of רב ינאי using a גזירה שוה of 'תוך' and 'עדה'

steps.title: But אסתר's case was public
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: אסתר's being taken by אחשורוש was public, so why didn't she give up her life?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a challenge from the story of אסתר. Her relationship with a non-Jewish king was known to everyone, so why was she not required to die rather than sin?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is built on the public rule just defined: in public, one must give up his life even over a lesser sin. אסתר's relationship with the king was known across the whole kingdom, yet she did not give up her life.

phrases.english: But wasn't Esther's case public?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the definition of public to challenge the rules from a known story.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that one must give up his life rather than sin, especially in public
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אסתר's relationship with אחשורוש was public and involved a forbidden relationship, yet she did not give up her life.

steps.title: אסתר was passive, like the ground
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that אסתר was 'קרקע עולם', a passive participant, so she did not have to give up her life.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: אסתר was like the ground of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers that אסתר did nothing active; she was like the ground that things are done upon. So the rule of giving up one's life did not apply to her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The obligation to die rather than sin applies to someone who actively does the sin. A woman who is only passive in the act is not required to give up her life. So the story of אסתר does not go against the rule; it is an exception.

keyTerms.meaning: Natural ground, meaning a passive participant

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, the rule of יהרג ואל יעבור applies to one who actively sins; a passive participant like אסתר is an exception. רבא gives a different answer in the next step.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Esther was like the natural ground.
phrases.notes: Like the ground, which doesn't do anything. He means she was completely passive.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: אֶסְתֵּר קַרְקַע עוֹלָם הָיְתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from אסתר in step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: an active sinner versus a passive participant
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since אסתר's case was public and involved a forbidden relationship, she should have had to give up her life.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because she was completely passive, she was not required to give up her life.

steps.title: רבא's different answer: acting for their own benefit is different
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers the question about אסתר differently from אביי. When the non-Jew acts for his own personal benefit, the rule is different.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: When the non-Jews act for their own pleasure, it is different.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second answer to why אסתר did not have to give up her life. It is a different answer from the one אביי gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי focused on אסתר: she was passive. רבא focuses on the non-Jew's motive. אחשורוש wanted her for his own pleasure, not to make a Jew break the תורה, so the public-sin rule of giving up one's life does not apply.
steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying the act became permitted in general. He is saying only that the obligation to give up one's life does not apply when the non-Jew acts for his own benefit.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Their own pleasure is different.
phrases.notes: He means: when the non-Jews force the sin only for their own benefit, not to make a Jew abandon the תורה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, independent answer to the קשיא about אסתר, alongside אביי's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the public-sin obligation applies only when the non-Jew intends to make the Jew violate the Torah.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any sin done in public, whatever the non-Jew's motive, requires giving up one's life, so אסתר should have done so.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because אחשורוש acted for his own pleasure, אסתר was not obligated to give up her life.

steps.title: Proof from handing over coal shovels
steps.stepSummary: רבא proves his rule from the accepted practice of giving coal shovels to the Persians, then applies the same reasoning to אסתר.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you do not say this, how do we give them the coal shovels? It must be that acting for their own benefit is different. Here too, with אסתר, acting for his own benefit is different.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא backs up his answer with a practice everyone already accepts. Jews handed over their coal shovels to the Persians and did not give up their lives to avoid it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Giving the Persians the shovels helped them in public, and the shovels were used at their religious festival, yet Jews did not give up their lives over it. The only explanation is that the Persians wanted the shovels for their own use, not to make Jews sin. The same reasoning applies to אחשורוש and אסתר.

keyTerms.meaning: for if you do not say so (introduces a proof)

phrases.english: For if you do not say so,
these coal shovels and fire pans,
phrases.notes: The Persians collected these from people's homes and used them to carry coals for their festival.

phrases.english: how do we give them to them?
Rather, their own pleasure is different.
Here too, their own pleasure is different.
phrases.notes: "Here" means the case of אסתר and אחשורוש.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי לָא תֵּימָא הָכִי, הָנֵי קְוָואקֵי וְדֵימוֹנִיקֵי הֵיכִי יָהֲבִינַן לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא's answer in step 9 with a proof from accepted practice.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that a non-Jew acting for his own benefit does not trigger the obligation to give up one's life.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The accepted practice of handing over coal shovels to the Persians without giving up one's life.

steps.title: רבא is consistent: cutting grass on Shabbat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that רבא follows the same reasoning in another ruling. If a non-Jew forces a Jew to cut grass on שבת for the non-Jew's animals, the Jew should cut it. If the grass is to be thrown into the river, the Jew should let himself be killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא follows his own reasoning, for רבא said: If a non-Jew tells a Jew, 'Cut grass on שבת and throw it to the animals, or I will kill you,' he should cut it and not be killed. If the non-Jew says, 'Throw it into the river,' he should be killed and not cut it. Why? Because the non-Jew wants to make him violate his religion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that רבא's answer about אסתר matches another ruling he gave elsewhere. This shows the idea is a consistent principle for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Feeding the animals helps the non-Jew, so it counts as his own benefit, and the Jew may sin rather than die. Throwing the grass into the river helps nobody. That shows the non-Jew only wants the Jew to break שבת, so the Jew must give up his life. Same act, different motive, different ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: and he follows his own reasoning
to make someone violate his religion

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, what decides the law is the non-Jew's motive. If he acts for his own benefit, the Jew does not have to die. If he acts to make the Jew violate the תורה, the Jew must die rather than sin.
steps.whyThisMatters: This case gives a clear test for the non-Jew's motive: does the forced act actually benefit him, or is it pointless except to make the Jew sin?

phrases.english: And Rava follows his own reasoning,
for Rava said:
A non-Jew who said to a certain Jew,
"Cut grass on Shabbat
and throw it to the animals,
and if not, I will kill you" –
he should cut, and not let him kill him.
If he said, "Throw it into the river" –
he should let him kill him, and not cut.
What is the reason?
He wants to make him violate his religion.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the principle רבא used for אסתר appears in another of his rulings.
steps.raayaObject: That רבא consistently holds that a non-Jew acting for his own benefit is different.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's ruling about a non-Jew forcing a Jew to cut grass on שבת.

steps.title: Is a non-Jew commanded to sanctify God's name?
steps.stepSummary: The Sages ask רבי אמי whether a בן נח is obligated in קידוש השם, meaning whether he must give up his life rather than sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked רבי אמי: Is a בן נח commanded about קידוש השם, or is he not commanded about קידוש השם?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. Until now it discussed when a Jew must die rather than sin. Now the Sages ask whether a non-Jew has the same obligation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בן נח has his own set of commandments. The question is whether, when he is forced to break one of them, he must give up his life the way a Jew sometimes must, or whether he may sin to stay alive.

keyTerms.meaning: a descendant of Noah, meaning a non-Jew
sanctifying God's name, by giving up one's life rather than sin

phrases.english: They asked Rabbi Ami:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּן נֹחַ מְצוֶּּוה עַל קְדוּשַּׁת הַשֵּׁם,
phrases.english: Is a descendant of Noah commanded about the sanctification of God's name,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵין מְצוֶּּוה עַל קְדוּשַּׁת הַשֵּׁם?
phrases.english: or is he not commanded about the sanctification of God's name?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the obligations of a Jew to a new question about a non-Jew.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a בן נח must give up his life rather than violate his commandments.

steps.title: אביי tries to prove from the seven מצוות of בני נח
steps.stepSummary: אביי argues that a בן נח is not commanded in קידוש השם, because the ברייתא counts only seven מצוות for בני נח, not eight.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Come and hear. The descendants of Noah were commanded seven מצוות. If they were also commanded to give up their lives, there would be eight!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי offers a proof that answers the question from step 12. He says a בן נח does not have to give up his life, because the list of his מצוות stops at seven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives a fixed number: seven מצוות for בני נח. If קידוש השם were also required of them, it would be an extra מצוה, and the count would be eight. Since the ברייתא says seven, אביי concludes that קידוש השם is not one of their obligations.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear. The גמרא is bringing a source as proof.
The seven מצוות all of mankind is commanded in.
And if it were so. This sets up a 'then it would follow' argument.

phrases.english: Abaye said: Come and hear:
The descendants of Noah were commanded seven מצוות.
And if it is so, there would be eight!
phrases.notes: If a בן נח really had to give up his life rather than sin, that would add one more מצוה to the list of seven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attempts to answer the question posed to רבי אמי in step 12.
steps.raayaObject: That a בן נח is not obligated in קידוש השם.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא stating that בני נח were commanded seven מצוות, a fixed count with no room for an eighth.

steps.title: רבא rejects the proof: the seven include all their details
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the seven מצוות include all the details connected to them, so קידוש השם could be part of one of the seven and not a separate eighth מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: The seven means the מצוות themselves together with all their attached details.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on אביי's proof. He says the number seven does not rule out קידוש השם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי assumed every obligation of a בן נח must be its own item in the count. רבא says each of the seven מצוות carries its related details with it. So giving up one's life rather than sin could be a detail inside an existing מצוה, such as the ban on עבודה זרה, and would not add an eighth.

keyTerms.meaning: Their accessories, meaning the related details and parts that come with each מצוה

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
They themselves and all their accessories.
phrases.notes: Literally 'accessories.' רבא means each of the seven comes packaged with its own details, so the count stays at seven.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: אִינְהוּ וְכֹל אַבְזְרַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects אביי's proof from the count of seven מצוות.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. רבא does not claim the opposite, that a בן נח is obligated.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: אביי wrongly assumed that every obligation must be counted as a separate מצוה. Details can be included within the seven.

steps.title: What is the final conclusion?
steps.stepSummary: Since אביי's proof was rejected, the גמרא asks what the final ruling is on whether a בן נח must give up his life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the final answer to the question about a בן נח. This line sets up the next step, where the answer comes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first attempt to settle the question failed, so the גמרא needs another source. The next step brings it.

keyTerms.meaning: What became of it? The phrase asks for the final conclusion on an open question.

phrases.english: What became of it?
phrases.notes: 'It' is the question asked of רבי אמי: must a בן נח give up his life rather than sin?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof in step 13 was rejected, the גמרא reopens the question for a final answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The final ruling on whether a בן נח is obligated in קידוש השם.

steps.title: The school of רב cites נעמן and אלישע
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה, quoting the school of רב, brings two פסוקים. In the first, נעמן asks forgiveness for bowing in the house of the idol רמון. In the second, אלישע answers him only 'Go in peace.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר אהבה said that the school of רב says: It is written that נעמן said, 'For this matter may ה׳ pardon your servant: when my master comes to the house of רמון to bow down there, and he leans on my hand, and I bow down.' And it is written, 'And he said to him: Go in peace.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the open question using the story of נעמן, a non-Jew. He told the נביא אלישע that he would have to bow in an idol's house alongside his master, and אלישע replied 'Go in peace.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: נעמן was a בן נח, and he was going to be forced to bow to an idol. אלישע did not tell him to give up his life. He simply said 'Go in peace.' The point being built is that if a בן נח were commanded in קידוש השם, אלישע would not have answered this way. So a בן נח is not commanded to give up his life. The next amud spells out this inference.

keyTerms.meaning: The school or study hall of רב
It is written. A פסוק is about to be quoted.
The house of רמון, a temple of an idol in ארם
Go in peace. These are אלישע's words to נעמן.

steps.whyThisMatters: This source is used to settle the question about non-Jews and giving up one's life. It shows a נביא responding calmly to a non-Jew who would be forced to bow to an idol.
steps.confusionAlert: Be careful not to think נעמן wanted to worship the idol. He was describing being forced by his master, the king, to bow alongside him.

phrases.english: Rav Adda bar Ahava said:
They say in the school of Rav: It is written:
"For this matter may ה׳ pardon your servant
phrases.notes: מלכים ב ה:יח. נעמן, the general of ארם, is speaking to אלישע.

phrases.english: when my master comes to the house of Rimmon
to bow down there
and he leans on my hand, and I bow down,"
And it is written: "And he said to him: Go in peace."
phrases.notes: מלכים ב ה:יט. This is אלישע's whole reply, with no warning to give up his life.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה: אָמְרִי בֵּי רַב, כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15 by bringing פסוקים.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The school of רב brings the story of נעמן. A non-Jew forced to bow to an idol received only 'Go in peace' from אלישע, with no demand that he give up his life.
